stops.name: Stuttgart, the dazzled and resentful court
stops.campa: He lives now in splendour at Stuttgart: coaches, jewels, fine houses, the confidence of a man at the summit. The court dazzles at his taste and hates his power; the burghers grumble; the clergy thunder that a Jew rules the treasury of a Christian land. Anti-Jewish placards and songs circulate. He trades offices, sells justice through the Fiscalamt, and lends at usury, and each act buys him money and an enemy in equal measure. He is the most powerful commoner in the duchy and the most exposed: a fortune built on a single life, the duke's.

stops.name: Stuttgart, appointed Geheimer Finanzrat
stops.campa: The duke raises him to Geheimer Finanzrat, privy finance councillor, the open acknowledgment of what all Württemberg already knows: that the Jew Oppenheimer is the true master of the state's money. Behind the scenes, Karl Alexander plots a deeper thing: to overturn the estate-constitution, break the Protestant Landstände, and tilt the duchy toward Catholic power: a coup by decree. Joseph Süß is the instrument of the finance without being told all of the plan. He has climbed as high as a court Jew can climb. There is nowhere left to go but down.

stops.name: Ludwigsburg Palace, the sudden death of Duke Karl Alexander
stops.campa: At Ludwigsburg, the great baroque palace, on the eve of a journey to inspect the frontier fortresses, Duke Karl Alexander is suddenly seized, a flood in the lungs, and at half past nine that night he is dead. In a single hour Joseph Süß loses everything: not a friend, but the one shield between him and a duchy of enemies. The plotted coup collapses; the Estates seize the moment they have prayed for. The protecting hand is cold, and the hunt begins before the body is.

stops.name: Ludwigsburg / Stuttgart, arrested that same night by Major von Röder
stops.campa: That very night Joseph Süß is taken. Major von Röder, sent to carry news of the death to the widowed duchess, induces the factor to ride with him, and on the road, or at its end, the trap closes. Before the sun rises the most powerful commoner in Württemberg is a prisoner. His houses are sealed, his papers seized, his fortune confiscated. The men he outranked yesterday are his jailers today. The Estates have their scapegoat: the Jew who can be blamed for every grievance the dead duke earned.

stops.name: Burg Hohenneuffen, solitary confinement in the mountain fortress
stops.campa: He is carried to Hohenneuffen, a vast fortress perched on a limestone crag high above the Swabian Alb, and shut in solitary confinement. From splendour to a stone cell in a week. Below the walls, the world he built is dismantled and turned into evidence. A commission of inquiry assembles; the Estates already know the verdict they want and set about manufacturing the crimes to fit it. In the cold heights of Hohenneuffen, alone, the sweet one begins the slow return to the God of his fathers that will mark his end.

stops.name: Festung Hohenasperg, transferred to the state prison
stops.campa: In May he is moved to Hohenasperg, the fortress-hill north of Stuttgart that Württemberg keeps for its most dangerous prisoners: the 'mountain of tears.' Here the interrogations grind on. He is accused of fraud, embezzlement, treason, usurpation of office, lechery with Christian women, bribery: a heap of charges, some true, some invented, none quite naming a capital crime. The lechery count is quietly dropped to spare the honour of noble ladies. The commission cannot find a law he has broken worthy of death, so they will invent the sentence and leave the crime vague.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the verdict of the inquisition-court
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of December the investigating court hands down death by hanging, for usurpation of office, fraud, lèse-majesté, and high treason. His appeal to the Imperial courts, his right under the Empire's law, is arbitrarily denied him. The trial is a mockery of every principle of justice, its outcome fixed from the first day by the Estates who needed a death. He is to hang not for a proven crime but for having been too powerful, too foreign, too useful to a hated duke: a Jew who wielded a Christian state's money.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the death-sentence signed by the regent Carl Rudolf
stops.campa: The administrator-regent Carl Rudolf sets his hand to the sentence on the twenty-fifth of January. The machinery of the state now turns only toward the gallows. A special scaffold is ordered built outside the city: an iron thing, monstrous and high, with a cage of iron to hold the body after. The theatre of the execution is designed in advance: not merely a hanging, but a spectacle, a warning, a purge. The scapegoat has been chosen, condemned, and now the altar is being raised for him on the road out of Stuttgart.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Herrenhaus am Marktplatz, the last cell
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of January he is brought down from Hohenasperg into Stuttgart itself, to the Herrenhaus by the market square, for his last days. Two clergymen and a baptized Jew, a lector from Tübingen, come at him without rest, pressing baptism upon him: convert, and perhaps be spared, and surely be saved. He refuses. In prison faith has returned to him; he prays, he fasts, he speaks the old prayers. A fellow Jew is permitted to visit on the eve, and finds him composed, resolved to die as what he was born.
stops.quote: Ich will als Jude sterben; mir geschieht Gewalt und Unrecht.
stops.quote_source: Traditional attribution, the martyr-line of the Jewish memory (his refusal of baptism and protest of the trial's injustice, both attested; the verbatim wording carried by later chronicle tradition, not a court transcript)

stops.name: Stuttgart, the procession to the Galgenberg on the Prag
stops.campa: On the fourth of February he is led out through the gates of Stuttgart, up the road toward the heights of the Prag, amid the rejoicing of thousands who have come to see the Jew hang. Broadsheets of the scene are already printed to be sold in the crowd. He walks composed. To the very foot of the ladder the ministers renew their assault, and to the very foot he refuses them, holding to the faith of his fathers against baptism, against the promise of life. The special iron gallows rises before him, red-painted, monstrous, waiting.

stops.name: The Galgenberg, hanged in the iron cage with the Shema on his lips
stops.campa: Upon the twelve-metre iron gallows they hoist him, and throttle him, and as the rope takes him Joseph Süß Oppenheimer cries out the first commandment of Israel: Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. The sweet one dies a Jew, refusing to the last breath the water that would have washed him into a Christian death. The Shema is his final word above the roaring crowd. The scapegoat is slain. The thread from Samuel Oppenheimer at Vienna finds its knot here, on the Prag, above Stuttgart.
stops.quote: Schma Jisrael, Adonai Elohenu, Adonai Echad. (Höre Israel, der Herr ist unser Gott, der Herr ist einer.)
stops.quote_source: Deuteronomy 6:4, recited on the gallows per the chronicles

stops.name: The Prag, the body left in the cage for six years
stops.campa: The corpse is locked in the iron cage and hoisted high on the gallows above the road, left to the wind and the crows and the gaze of every traveller entering Stuttgart. For six years it hangs there, a rotting warning, a thing of horror and pilgrimage. The Jews of the region are expelled, briefly, in the same convulsion. Not until 1744, when the young Duke Carl Eugen comes of age, is the cage taken down and the remains at last buried beneath the gallows. The man is gone; the legend is only beginning.
